OPINION

I Was an Airborne Cameraman for Decades. This Is Why We Need to Retire News Choppers

We are mourning the losses from NBC4 and Telemundo 52’s recent helicopter crash, yet not asking the question: Is the benefit of in-air reporting worth the risk?

By Scott ShulmanSeptember 28, 2026, 6 minute read

ShareCopy link

What began as a fatal carjacking on January 3, 1992, at 10:30 a.m., in Central California became the catalyst for change in local television that redefined live coverage of breaking news.

Although newsrooms have had access to helicopters for years, it wasn’t until Darren Michael Stroh led police on a 300-mile pursuit that the public developed a hunger for live pictures of a dramatic, high-speed chase.

When they crossed the L.A. County line, local news helicopters picked up the chase, broadcasting pictures live. Stroh eventually slowed to a crawl as he ran out of gas on a Westminster freeway offramp.

I remember it as though it was yesterday, because I was the cameraman who shot it from the KABC helicopter.

It didn’t take long before high-speed police pursuits became a staple of local news. Stations regularly interrupt programming to bring viewers these Roman Colosseum-style spectacles delivered right to their home screen.

As a witness to this man’s death, I became an active participant. It troubles me that my role in bringing the horrific scene to viewers helped fuel a thirst for more.

When UPS delivered my Golden Mike, I pitched it—three-pointer style—into the trash bin.
